entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Maha Sawa or Trà Hòa bố để was a king of Champa from 1342 to 1360. When his brother-in-law Che Anan died in 1342, Tra Hoa claimed the throne.

As king, Maha Sawa implemented various reforms aimed at strengthening Champa's position in Southeast Asia. He invested in infrastructure, including the construction of roads and bridges, and encouraged trade with neighboring kingdoms.

Maha Sawa's reign also saw the rise of Buddhism in Champa, as he actively supported the spread of the religion and built several temples and monasteries. This had a lasting impact on the cultural identity of Champa and its people.

Despite his efforts, Maha Sawa's reign was cut short when he died in 1360. His successor, Che Anan's brother, took over and continued to build on Maha Sawa's legacy.

Maha Sawa's legacy extends beyond his own reign, as he played a key role in shaping Champa's relations with neighboring kingdoms and contributed to the spread of Buddhism in the region.
